findings.title: Migration crashes when the legacy embed category has no matching category
findings.body: The category lookup assumes the join always returns a row and immediately dereferences `...[0]['id']`. On installations where `embed_category` was left at its default blank value (or its site-setting row was never persisted), the join returns no rows, so this raises before the intended `category_id == 0` fallback can run. This blocks the entire deployment migration for the common unconfigured case.

findings.title: Legacy URL-form host entries are copied in a form the new lookup can never match
findings.body: The old setting accepted entries such as `http://discourse.org` and `https://example.com/path` (the previous lookup explicitly parsed these forms), but this raw INSERT stores them unchanged. The new `EmbeddableHost.record_for_host` extracts only `URI(host).host` and compares it to the stored `host`, so a row containing `http://discourse.org` or a path will never match `discourse.org`. The model normalization callback is bypassed by this SQL INSERT, causing existing configured embeds to be denied after migration.

findings.title: Duplicate host mappings make the destination category ambiguous
findings.body: Neither the model nor the migration enforces uniqueness of a host, while `record_for_host` resolves a match with an unordered `.first`. Administrators can create the same hostname more than once with different categories (including case variants), after which imports for that host are assigned to whichever row the database happens to return rather than to a deterministic configured relationship. Add a case-insensitive uniqueness constraint/index and validation, or define an explicit conflict policy.

findings.title: Hosts with ports are accepted but can never be authorized
findings.body: The validation permits values such as `example.com:8080`, and the normalization callback leaves the port in the stored value. `record_for_host` then parses a request URL and compares only `URI(...).host` (`example.com`) against the stored string (`example.com:8080`), so no referer or retrieval URL can match that saved configuration. Either reject ports or normalize/query them consistently.

findings.title: Updating or deleting a missing host raises a server error
findings.body: Both `update` and `destroy` use `where(...).first` but dereference the result without checking it. A request for an ID that was deleted by another admin session, or simply does not exist, calls `save_host(nil)` or `nil.destroy` and returns a 500 instead of a 404. This also leaves the admin UI without a recoverable response for concurrent edits/deletes.
